\chapter{Child, Son, Daughter}
\label{ch:ml-child-son-daughter}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say child, son and daughter in Malayalam, and say which of the three matches Tamil most closely and which one Kannada softened.}

Say ithu ente makalaanu, set makan/makal beside Tamil's identical makan/makal and Kannada's softened maga/magalu, and ask ninte makanu ethra vayassundu using Chapter 19's dative-subject question again.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuṭṭi]{\ml{കുട്ടി} (kuṭṭi) — \textquotedblleft{}child, kid,\textquotedblright{} the general word before the specific ones}

\label{lesson:ML-C36-kutti}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Suhṛttŭ} named someone you choose. This chapter turns to someone you don't — the people a family is built around.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}} — \emph{kuṭṭi} — \textbf{child, kid}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{കുട്ടിയാണ്}.} — \emph{ithu ente kuṭṭiyāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my child.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}} is the general word — any child, before you say whose son or daughter.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}} is native Dravidian, matching Tamil's \textbf{\ta{குட்டி}} (\emph{kuṭṭi}) closely. Both languages let the same word cover two things: a human child, and the young of an animal — a \textbf{\ml{പൂച്ചക്കുട്ടി}} (\emph{pūccakkuṭṭi}) is a kitten, built on \textbf{\ml{പൂച്ച}}, \textquotedblleft{}cat,\textquotedblright{} met earlier in this book, the same way \textbf{kuṭṭi} attaches to any animal name for its young. English does something similar with \textquotedblleft{}kid,\textquotedblright{} which covers both a child and a baby goat — one small word, carrying the same double duty in two unrelated language families.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ithu ente kuṭṭiyāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — this is my child
  \item the animal sense — \textquotedblleft{}pūcca … pūccakkuṭṭi\textquotedblright{} — cat, kitten
  \item the family and the friend, once more — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumbaṁ … suhṛttŭ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the six family people-words, and the group word — \textquotedblleft{}acchan, amma … kuṭumbaṁ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my child.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ithu ente kuṭṭiyāṇŭ}.) What two things can \emph{kuṭṭi} mean? (\textbf{A human child}, or \textbf{the young of an animal} — like \emph{pūccakkuṭṭi}, kitten.) Which English word carries the very same double duty? (\textbf{Kid}.) Name the six family people-words once more, and the group word none of them supplied. (\emph{Acchan, amma, cēṭṭan, aniyan, cēcci, aniyatti} — and \textbf{kuṭumbaṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[makan]{\ml{മകൻ} (makan) — \textquotedblleft{}son,\textquotedblright{} a word Tamil hardly changed at all}

\label{lesson:ML-C36-makan}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kuṭṭi} was the general word. Now the two specific ones — starting with the son.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{മകൻ}} — \emph{makan} — \textbf{son}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{മകനാണ്}.} — \emph{ithu ente makanāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my son.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{മകൻ}} continues \textbf{Proto-Dravidian *makan}, \textquotedblleft{}son.\textquotedblright{} Tamil keeps almost the identical shape, \textbf{\ta{மகன்}} (\emph{makan}) — same consonants, same vowels, same final \emph{-n}. Kannada moved further: the \emph{-k-} between vowels softened to \emph{-g-}, and the final \emph{-n} dropped, giving \textbf{\ka{ಮಗ}} (\emph{maga}). So on this word it is Malayalam and Tamil that hold the older, more conservative shape, and Kannada that innovated — the same closeness the very first greetings already showed in \emph{nandi}, \emph{athe}, \emph{illa} and \emph{śari}, this time in a family word rather than a greeting.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ithu ente makanāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — this is my son
  \item the two cousins — \textquotedblleft{}makan\textquotedblright{} (Malayalam, Tamil) … \textquotedblleft{}maga\textquotedblright{} (Kannada)
  \item general then specific — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭṭi … makan\textquotedblright{}
  \item the friend-word, once more — \textquotedblleft{}suhṛttŭ\textquotedblright{} — su plus hṛd
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my son.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ithu ente makanāṇŭ}.) Which sister keeps almost the identical word? (\textbf{Tamil} — \emph{makan}.) What did Kannada change? (\textbf{Softened \emph{-k-} to \emph{-g-}} and \textbf{dropped the final \emph{-n}}, giving \emph{maga}.) What does \emph{suhṛttŭ} literally mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Good-heart\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{su} plus \emph{hṛd}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[makaḷ]{\ml{മകൾ} (makaḷ) — \textquotedblleft{}daughter,\textquotedblright{} the closest match yet}

\label{lesson:ML-C36-makal}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Makan} matched Tamil closely. Its pair matches even closer — and gives you a reason to ask an old question again.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{മകൾ}} — \emph{makaḷ} — \textbf{daughter}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{മകളാണ്}.} — \emph{ithu ente makaḷāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my daughter.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{മകൾ}} continues \textbf{Proto-Dravidian *makaḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}daughter.\textquotedblright{} Tamil's \textbf{\ta{மகள்}} (\emph{makaḷ}) is not just close — it is \textbf{identical}, sound for sound. Kannada shows the same softening you just met in \emph{maga}: \textbf{\ka{ಮಗಳು}} (\emph{magaḷu}), \emph{-k-} to \emph{-g-}, plus a closing \emph{-u}. So where \emph{makan}/\emph{makan} was already a close match, \emph{makaḷ}/\emph{makaḷ} is the closer one still — two sisters holding one Proto-Dravidian root letter for letter, four thousand years and a script apart.

Now that you have a son and a daughter, the age question comes back with someone new to ask it about: \textbf{ninṟe makanŭ ethra vayassuṇṭŭ?} — \textquotedblleft{}how old is your son?\textquotedblright{} — the same dative-subject-plus-\emph{uṇṭŭ} shape, unchanged.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ithu ente makaḷāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — this is my daughter
  \item the identical pair — \textquotedblleft{}makaḷ, makaḷ\textquotedblright{} — Malayalam, Tamil
  \item son, daughter, both cousins — \textquotedblleft{}makan … maga; makaḷ … magaḷu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the age question, asked again — \textquotedblleft{}ninṟe makanŭ ethra vayassuṇṭŭ?\textquotedblright{}
  \item general, then specific, twice over — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭṭi … makan … makaḷ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my daughter.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ithu ente makaḷāṇŭ}.) How closely does Tamil match this word, compared with \emph{makan}? (\textbf{Even closer} — \emph{makaḷ} is \textbf{identical} sound for sound, where \emph{makan} only nearly matched.) Ask \textquotedblleft{}how old is your son?\textquotedblright{} using the age question's shape. (\emph{Ninṟe makanŭ ethra vayassuṇṭŭ?} — \textquotedblleft{}to your son, how much age exists?\textquotedblright{}) What is the general word for a child, before \emph{makan} or \emph{makaḷ}? (\textbf{\ml{കുട്ടി}}, \emph{kuṭṭi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bha]{\ml{ഭ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S129-letter-bha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ൃ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only — and it has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഭ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഭ}} — \emph{bha}.

It is a \textbf{consonant} carrying its own \emph{a}, and its sound is a \emph{b} with a puff of breath after it — \textbf{bha}, not \emph{ba}.

Three words you have already used are built on it, and all three come from the Sanskrit layer.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ശുഭ}} \emph{śubha} — good, auspicious — the first half of your evening and night greetings
  \item \textbf{\ml{പ്രഭാതം}} \emph{prabhātaṁ} — dawn, inside \textbf{\ml{സുപ്രഭാതം}} \emph{suprabhātaṁ}
  \item \textbf{\ml{കുംഭം}} \emph{kuṁbhaṁ} — the month, met with the calendar
\end{itemize}

Say each one and listen for the breath: \emph{śu-bha}, \emph{pra-bhā-taṁ}, \emph{kuṁ-bhaṁ}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ഭ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ഭ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{ഭ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{ശുഭ}  ·  \ml{പ്രഭാതം}  ·  \ml{കുംഭം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{ഭ} three times, saying \emph{bha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{ഭ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{ഭ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{bha}}.) Which greeting of yours starts with it?
\end{tcolorbox}
